Industry observers note that xabi Alonso is straying towards crisis territory. Here’s a mind-bending statistic: Chelsea are eighth but have now lost more league games than Manchester United. They were bullied by a rampant Leeds United, who fully merited their first win at Stamford Bridge since going top with a 2-0 victory in December 1999, and can look forward to another season with no European football if they do not sharpen up soon.

Recent findings suggest that it is not really worth dwelling on the fact that the second Leeds goal, a Dominic Calvert-Lewin penalty converted early in an astonishingly one-sided second half, came after Morgan Rogers was harshly penalised for handball. That was a minor detail given the wider picture. Leeds, superbly coached by Daniel Farke and up to sixth after two clinical strikes from Noah Okafor, Calvert-Lewin’s sixth goal of the season and a late effort from Brenden Aaronson, were so dominant that they had no real need for a helping hand from the officials.

Farke’s side were tactically superior against flimsy opposition. For Chelsea, who were jeered off after their fifth defeat in 11 games, the indignities piled high. Records are falling, but not in a good way. This is the first time in 67 years they have lost grudge matches at home to Leeds and Tottenham in the same season, leaving Alonso on shaky ground with supporters, and there was further alarm when Cole Palmer appeared to clash with Willie Isa after the side’s “cultural architect” urged Chelsea’s No 10 to acknowledge the crowd at full-time.

Palmer cut a disgruntled figure throughout and did nothing to make Thomas Tuchel rethink his decision to leave him out of the England squad. The one mitigating factor is that few players will thrive in a directionless team. What does Alonso want Chelsea to be? No one knows. There are no patterns of play and the main takeaway from this surrender is that the only sign of an identity was an addiction to calamitous defending.

Sources indicate that calvert-Lewin followed the lead of Sunderland’s Brian Brobbey by tormenting Levi Colwill and Wesley Fofana. Alonso was appointed in the summer but the pressure is mounting already. The Spaniard’s control even let him down when a ball dropped towards the technical area in the second half.

Recent findings suggest that it was some turnaround from the visitors, who trailed when Emmanuel Emegha marked his full debut by scoring his first goal since joining Chelsea from Strasbourg last summer. Farke continues to excel. The best that can be noted of Alonso is that he needs time. Losing Moisés Caicedo early on was a blow. Even then it is impossible to understand Alonso’s intended style of play. There is an emptiness to Chelsea. They faced 21 shots and failed to up the physicality after crumbling against Sunderland.

Industry observers note that admittedly Alonso is dealing with João Pedro’s absence in attack. He has toyed with a false nine in recent weeks, but used a target man this time and the early signs were promising. Emegha gave Chelsea a focal point and finished well when an error from James Justin allowed Rogers to send the striker through on goal.

Leeds were on top when they conceded. Chelsea had lost Caicedo, who made way for Jordan Henderson after injuring his back in a collision with Justin, and were already wobbling. Calvert-Lewin spurned three excellent headed chances and Leeds levelled after 28 minutes.

In a recent development, chelsea had no defensive leaders. Fofana is too easily ruffled in the air and was involved in the equaliser. He sent a routine header back into dangerous territory and Chelsea panicked. Josh Acheampong mistimed his jump as the ball bounced around and Calvert-Lewin was able to find Okafor, who cut inside and slipped a low shot past Emiliano Martínez.

Sources indicate that farke was rightly disappointed that Leeds were not ahead at half-time. Tarik Muharemovic charged forward from defence, away from Palmer’s feeble challenge, and crossed for Calvert-Lewin to flick wide. Ethan Ampadu ran midfield, outshining Henderson and Romeo Lavia, and the Leeds wing-backs were wonderful. Ao Tanaka went close and Muharemovic grimaced after having a goal disallowed for offside.

Alonso looked bewildered. Colwill, low on confidence since returning from a knee injury, kept misplacing simple passes and Estêvão Willian was ineffective on the right. Chelsea were jeered off and made a dreadful start to the second half. Martínez should have conceded a penalty for a challenge on Calvert-Lewin. Michael Oliver then pointed to the spot when Rogers was adjudged to have handled Jayden Bogle’s shot.

• Leeds have won their first game against Chelsea at Stamford Bridge in all competitions since December 1999, ending a run of 10 away games against the Blues without victory (D2 L8), while they’ve scored 4+ goals away at Chelsea for the first time since January 1970 (5-2).

Industry observers note that it looked harsh given Rogers’ arm was close to his body and the ball hit him close to the shoulder but the decision was upheld after a VAR check. Calvert-Lewin stepped up to score and the result was never in doubt once Leeds led. Chelsea, who were mentally fragile, crumbled. Leeds were rampant. Chelsea could not cope with Ampadu’s long throws. One was half cleared but Sean Longstaff worked the ball back to Ampadu, who crossed for Okafor to make it 3-1.

“We are in a fragile moment mentally,” Alonso noted. “When we receive a punch we didn’t recover. The fans were disappointed because the expectations are high. I understand their disappointment. There were moments that we were not competing at the level required.”.

In a recent development, the closing stages were miserable for Chelsea, who have already conceded 20 goals. Leeds cruised and completed the humiliation when Aaronson, a late substitute, turned past Malo Gusto before sliding a shot through Martínez’s grasp.

The home sections had already emptied out. Those who stayed soon made their displeasure clear.

German economy returns to growth, so why is the country still worried?

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Is Germany's economy back on the up?
  • At the 2026 Mechanical Engineering Summit in Berlin this week, the mood was sullen.
  • It has been revealed that the mechanical and plant engineering sector was the backbone of German industry for decades.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Is Germany's economy back on the up? The answer to that question depends on your perspective.

At the 2026 Mechanical Engineering Summit in Berlin this week, the mood was sullen. "A year ago, I mentioned here: We are angry. Today I must say: We are stunned," Bertram Kawlath, president of the Mechanical Engineering Industry Association (VDMA), said in his opening remarks on Tuesday.

It has been revealed that the mechanical and plant engineering sector was the backbone of German industry for decades. It once employed more than a million people; now 15,000 positions are being cut every month. Production has shrunk about 20% since 2018.

Kawlath criticized the federal government's infighting and lack of reform, as well as what the companies consider a continued high bureaucracy and tax burden.

"[We are] stunned by the whitewashing in so many government statements. Stunned by the increasingly visible decline of our country as a business location.".

Industry observers note that german Chancellor Friedrich Merz promised quick reforms and a rapidly noticeable economic upswing when he took office in May 2025. A year and a half later, reality has caught up with him.

Merz's coalition of his conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU), its Bavarian sister party the Christian Social Union, (CSU), along with the center-left Social Democrats(SPD), keeps running into trouble. In addition, there are crises and wars. The German economy is facing more headwinds than seldom before, Merz said in October at the German Employers' Day conference in Berlin.

Industry observers note that given the circumstances, small successes are even more meaningful. "A heartfelt thanks for the good news you bring," Merz mentioned when he received the autumn report of the Council of Economic Experts in Berlin, which predicted economic growth of 1.3% for 2026 and 1% for 2027.

Industry observers note that the economic experts have a German government mandate to independently analyze business activity and make recommendations for economic policy. Earlier this year, they were much more pessimistic.

"The German economy has recovered quicker than expected from the energy price shock sparked by the war in Iran," remarked Monika Schnitzer, chair of the expert advisory board, explaining the prognosis. "We see a significant economic recovery, driven by surprisingly strong exports and high government spending.".

Sources indicate that the chancellor, who celebrated his 71st birthday on November 11, spoke of "encouraging signals" in his address. "The economy in Germany is slowly on the rise again. Considering the many crises in Germany, it was not totally expected that we would manage that.".

But these improved prospects do not change the long-term problems. An ageing society means the bills for pensions, health and caregiving are constantly rising.

Industry observers note that at the same time, the number of working-age people who finance these services is sinking. That puts increasing pressure on the public purse. According to Berlin's financial planning, social welfare costs, defense and interest on debt will account for 80% of the spending in the federal government's budget.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

According to recent reports, "We must realize that in the long term the expected revenues in the federal budget will not be enough to cover the planned expenses," Schnitzer warned. The growth rates are far below what is needed to secure the same level of prosperity as previous decades in the long term.

"To grow out of this budgetary predicament, we would need levels of economic growth which we haven't experienced in Germany for the past 50 years," she said.

It has been revealed that the government is at the moment in final deliberations over its 2027 budget; spending upwards of €555 billion ($615 billion) is planned. Because revenue won't be enough to cover it, the government is planning to take on more than €118 billion in upcoming debt. Adding the debt-financed special funds for infrastructure and the military, the new borrowing adds up to almost €204 billion.

The economic experts have warned that if Germany continues with this path, the debt-to-GDP ratio could rise to 100% by 2040. This ratio indicates how high the national debt is in relation to annual economic output. At the end of 2025, it was 63.5%.

Germany is the only country of the world's leading democratic industrialized nations (G7) to still hold a AAA rating, the best possible credit rating in finance markets. It signals to investors the smallest possible default risk for German government bonds. "I want it to stay that way," Merz emphasized.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

According to recent reports, however, taking on less debt will not be simple. "A reduction in debt-based financing presents policymakers with a consolidation task of historic proportions and will require tough decisions," said Schnitzer. The belt-tightening must, however, be designed to enable growth. Some recommendations include reducing environmentally harmful tax benefits — like the energy tax breaks for diesel fuel.

It has been revealed that the so-called "mothers' pension", a pension subsidy for older parents, should be revoked, said the experts. Tax increases could become necessary in the medium term, for example with value-added tax.

"The burden should be shared fairly between generations and societal groups," Schnitzer said.

According to recent reports, according to the chancellor, the experts' message has been received. Solid state finances are an issue in Germany but also throughout the European Union. Merz said there needs to be a consolidation course, adding that politicians have a duty to the younger generation. Reforms are needed, especially when it comes to social security systems.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

It has been revealed that economic researchers are setting their hopes on increasing companies' productivity. Put simply, productivity describes how much a company can generate with its employees, machinery and resources in a set time.

Sources indicate that according to the Council of Economic Experts, there is enormous variation even within the same industries. In Germany, the top companies are up to five times as productive as the weakest enterprises.

Sources indicate that if the less productive companies caught up, economic growth could increase significantly, it stated in the report. "Fresh technologies and business models could drive peak productivity and allow new highly productive companies to develop.".

But innovations need capital. It's here that the Ifo Economic Research Institute sees considerable deficiencies.

Latest evaluations show that German universities produce significantly fewer successful business startups than their counterparts in the United Kingdom or United States. For example, for every 1,000 students, about 14 venture capital-backed founders emerge from the vicinity of Stanford University each year. In Cambridge, the European leader, it's 3.5. In Munich, by contrast, it's only 0.5.

There continues to be an abundance of inventors and tinkerers in Germany, especially in mechanical engineering. However, the message from the industry summit in Berlin was that for renewed success, labor costs must come down. Suggestions included longer working hours and more flexibility for employers around job protection.

Industry observers note that the intention was not to cut employees' wages and salaries. However, a latest study by the German Economic Institute commissioned for the German Mechanical Engineering Industry Association showed that extending the working week by an hour alone would increase real gross domestic product by 1.5% in the coming five years.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A consistent daily routine may do more for your health than you realize.
  • In a recent development, the findings suggest that everyday habits, such as waking up, eating meals, socializing, and going to bed at consistent times, may play an notable role in physical and mental well-being.
  • The discovery could be especially crucial for older adults, who frequently experience sleep difficulties.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A consistent daily routine may do more for your health than you realize. Researchers at the University of Missouri have found that older adults who follow regular daily schedules tend to experience less physical pain and fewer symptoms of depression, even when they struggle to get a good night's sleep.

In a recent development, the findings suggest that everyday habits, such as waking up, eating meals, socializing, and going to bed at consistent times, may play an notable role in physical and mental well-being. By helping the body maintain its natural internal clock, a predictable routine could offer health benefits that extend beyond improved sleep.

The discovery could be especially crucial for older adults, who frequently experience sleep difficulties. According to the National Council on Aging, roughly half of adults age 60 and older report symptoms of insomnia, a condition that can make it difficult to fall asleep, stay asleep, or get restful sleep.

Daily Routines Linked to Less Pain and Depression.

Sources indicate that to investigate the relationship between sleep, daily habits, and overall health, Eunjin Tracy, an assistant professor in the College of Education and Human Development at the University of Missouri, examined survey responses from 67 older adults. Among the participants, 37 reported experiencing insomnia.

It has been revealed that as researchers expected, those with insomnia generally reported more physical pain and higher levels of depression than participants without the condition. However, another pattern emerged when Tracy examined their daily routines.

It has been revealed that participants who maintained more consistent schedules tended to report less pain and fewer depressive symptoms, regardless of their sleep quality. This suggests that keeping regular daily habits may be associated with better health even when sleep problems persist.

Industry observers note that "Regardless of sleep quality, those who reported having a regular daily routine had lower levels of physical pain and less depression compared to those without a daily routine," Tracy mentioned. "If we are consistent with when we wake up, eat, work or study, interact with others and go to bed, those time cues help synchronize our internal body clocks. Over the long term, that seems to be linked with improved health outcomes.".

Why Your Body's Internal Clock Matters.

Recent findings suggest that one possible explanation involves the circadian rhythm, the body's natural 24-hour timing system. This internal clock helps coordinate when we feel awake or sleepy and influences numerous biological processes, including hormone activity, metabolism, and mood.

Rather than operating independently of our surroundings, the circadian system responds to signals that help it keep time. Light and darkness are especially important, but regular activities such as eating, working, interacting with others, and sleeping can also provide timing cues.

Industry observers note that when these signals follow a predictable pattern, they help keep the body's biological rhythms aligned. Irregular schedules, on the other hand, can interfere with that coordination.

"When we regulate our circadian rhythm well, our bodies function well, but if it gets too distracted, our bodies don't function as well," Tracy said.

Although the study did not establish that regular routines directly reduce pain or depression, the findings point to circadian regulation as one possible explanation for the connection.

The Hidden Effects of Social Jet Lag.

Sources indicate that even relatively small changes in daily schedules may disrupt the body's internal clock. One common example is social jet lag, which occurs when a person's sleep schedule shifts between workdays and days off.

Someone who wakes up early throughout the week but stays up late and sleeps in on weekends may experience this mismatch. The resulting disruption resembles some of the effects of traveling across time zones, even though the person has never left home.

Tracy suggests that maintaining reasonably consistent schedules throughout the entire week, including weekends, may help limit these disruptions and support healthier circadian rhythms.

"As someone who wakes up and goes to bed at the same time every day, I think a daily routine can be helpful for people of all ages across their lifespan," Tracy said. "There is growing awareness about the concept of social jet lag -- waking up and going to bed at different times on weekends compared to weekdays -- and the disruptions it causes to our circadian rhythm, so hopefully this research helps more people consider the health benefits of a daily routine. Since one-third of our lives will be spent sleeping, I think health and well-being research should be looked at holistically from a 24-hour perspective and not just focus on when we are awake.".

A Simple Habit With Potential Health Benefits.

In a recent development, the research highlights an aspect of healthy living that can be easy to overlook. While getting enough quality sleep remains vital, the consistency of activities throughout the day may also be connected to how people feel physically and emotionally.

Industry observers note that because the study relied on survey data from a relatively small group of older adults, it cannot prove that adopting a regular routine will relieve pain or depression. Larger studies would be needed to establish whether changing daily schedules directly improves these outcomes.

Still, the findings suggest that a predictable daily routine may be a useful component of a broader approach to health, particularly for people experiencing insomnia.

For older adults and potentially people of other ages, simple habits such as maintaining regular waking times, eating meals on a consistent schedule, and limiting major changes in weekend sleep patterns may help support the body's natural rhythms.

The study, "Behavioral-social rhythms and insomnia symptoms: associations with pain, body mass index, and depressive symptoms among older adults," was published in the Journal of Behavioral Medicine.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • China has debuted a cybersecurity probe into Micron Technology, one of America’s largest memory chip makers, in apparent retaliation after US allies in Asia and Europe revealed upcoming restrictions on the sale of key technology to Beijing.
  • The Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC) will review products sold by Micron in the country, according to a statement by the watchdog late on Friday.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

China has debuted a cybersecurity probe into Micron Technology, one of America’s largest memory chip makers, in apparent retaliation after US allies in Asia and Europe revealed upcoming restrictions on the sale of key technology to Beijing.

The Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC) will review products sold by Micron in the country, according to a statement by the watchdog late on Friday.

The move is aimed at “ensuring the security of key information infrastructure supply chains, preventing cybersecurity risks caused by hidden product problems, and maintaining national security,” it noted.

It came on the same day that Japan, a US ally, stated it would restrict the export of advanced chip manufacturing equipment to countries including China, following similar moves by the United States and the Netherlands.

Washington and its allies have unveiled curbs on China’s semiconductor industry, which strike at the heart of Beijing’s bid to become a tech superpower.

Last month, the Netherlands also unveiled new restrictions on overseas sales of semiconductor technology, citing the need to protect national security. In October, the United States banned Chinese companies from buying advanced chips and chipmaking equipment without a license.

Micron told CNN it was aware of the review.

Recent findings suggest that “We are in communication with the CAC and are cooperating fully,” it noted, adding that it stands by the security of its products. “Micron’s product shipments, engineering, manufacturing, sales and other functions are operating as normal.”.

Shares in Micron sank 4.4% on Wall Street Friday following the news, the biggest drop in more than three months. On Monday, they closed another 1.2% lower. Micron derives more than 10% of its revenue from China.

In an earlier filing, the Idaho-based organization had warned of such risks.

“The Chinese government may restrict us from participating in the China market or may prevent us from competing effectively with Chinese companies,” it noted last week.

Japan joins the US and Europe in chipmaking curbs on China.

China has strongly criticized restrictions on tech exports, saying last month it “firmly opposes” such measures.

According to recent reports, in efforts to boost growth and job creation, Beijing is seeking to woo foreign investments as it grapples with mounting economic challenges. The newly minted premier Li Qiang and several top economic officials have been rolling out the welcome wagon for global CEOs and promising they would “provide a good environment and services.”.

But Beijing has also exerted growing pressure on foreign companies to bring them into line with its agenda.

Last month, authorities closed the Beijing office of Mintz Group, a US corporate intelligence firm, and detained five local staff.

Days earlier, they suspended Deloitte’s operations in Beijing for three months and imposed a fine of $31 million over alleged lapses in its work auditing a state-owned distressed debt manager.

CNN’s Michelle Toh, Junko Ogura, Sandi Sidhu and Chris Lau contributed to the article.

Alex Consani is ready for a spin around Vice City.

With the supermodel lending her voice to Grand Theft Auto VI—which is poised to be the biggest video game of the year after making $3.79 billion in preorder and first-day sales, according to parent company Take Two—it was only appropriate that she channel that car vibe into her clutch look for the game’s launch party.

According to recent reports, consani buckled up for the Nov. 18 event at the Gekko restaurant in Miami wearing a short dress from Paris-based label Sevali’s spring 2025 collection that was made out of upcycled seatbelts. The belts crisscrossed around the 23-year-old’s svelte figure, coming to a click—literally—with a buckle that was strapped across her shoulder.

The Victoria’s Secret model completed her look with clear kitten heels and her long blonde hair parted down the middle and flowing behind her.

In the newly released video game, Consani can be heard as a DJ for the in-game radio station Flash FM alongside singer Robyn. The two play songs from the likes of Olivia Rodrigo, Charli XCX, Zara Larsson and more as they put their commentary into high gear.

After playing Rodrigo’s “good 4 u,” Consani can be heard saying in a clip posted from the game, “How do you even fumble a baddie like Olivia?”.

She also had some love for Charli XCX, saying, “Whatever Charli XCX does, she’s my medicine. That is my f--king doctor, y’all.”.

In a recent development, as for Larsson? After playing the Swedish singer’s hit “Fast Emotion,” Consani commented, “God, I love Zara so much.”.

Of course, the model isn’t the only star to lend her voice to GTA VI, with Bad Bunny coming in as host of Latin radio Cocoteo FM, PinkPantheress DJing the indie dance station Stockyard FM, “Weird” Al Yankovic hosting the ’80s station Vice City FM, Morgan Wallen and Lana Del Rey co-hosting Back Country Radio and Rolling Stones guitarist Keith Richards playing his part as DJ Keith on Gloriana Blues Radio.

Grand Theft Auto VI marks the latest installment in the long-running video game series, coming out 13 years after the record-breaking Grand Theft Auto V.

The latest game features characters like Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos as they take part in fan-favorite activities from previous games like car-jackings, shootouts, street-racing, robberies, swimming, jet-skiing, sky-diving, visiting the strip club and, yes, even petting dogs. GTA 6 is set around locations inspired by Floria, allowing players new playable vehicles like kayaks and airboats to roam around the new locale.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If Mikel Arteta was delighted to see the back of Eddie Howe as Newcastle’s head coach, the bad news is that another similarly awkward technical area adversary has been installed at St James’ Park.

In a recent development, arsenal’s manager never seemed to relish trips to face Howe’s old team and he certainly did not enjoy this latest trip to Tyneside, where Matthias Jaissle’s initially overwhelmed team fought back commendably to earn a point courtesy of a stellar second-half performance. At half-time the crowd had felt close to turning against Jaissle but he held his nerve and, thanks to a triple substitution and subtle tactical rejig suggested he is no mug after all.

It left Arsenal – who lost their outstanding goalkeeper David Raya to a potentially significant second-half shoulder injury – still top of the Premier League, six points clear of Brighton and Manchester City, and Arteta with a face like thunder.

It has been revealed that just last week Bruno Guimarães claimed he was “beloved” by Newcastle fans but the club’s former captain turned Arsenal midfielder found himself serenaded by a soundtrack of boos of the sort usually reserved for Sunderland players. Newcastle’s problem is that, despite spending about £275m this summer, they have struggled to replace last season’s departed star trio – Guimarães, Sandro Tonali and Anthony Gordon.

In a recent development, that reality perhaps left Howe’s successor – who arrived just before the start of the season – making a not so subtle point with his team sheet here. Of Jaissle’s starting XI only the goalkeeper, Lukas Hornicek, the right-back Amar Dedic and the midfielder Sean Steur were close-season signings.

The other five new faces were either benched (Nico González and Matias Fernandez-Pardo) or did not make the 20-man matchday squad (Aladji Bamba and Bazoumana Touré). Admittedly Ewen Jaouen is injured but, given Bamba and Toure cost a combined £78.5m, their omission represented quite a statement. Ditto the decision to bench González and Fernandez-Pardo and their individual £50m plus price tag.

Meanwhile the jury remains out on Hornicek. The Czech international has made some excellent saves this season but, initially here, his kicking proved pretty much uniformly poor and he was fortunate to be reprieved after hesitating too long as the impressive Kai Havertz closed in.

Jaissle’s frustration with his goalkeeper proved well apparent as Arsenal took increasing control of a first half that saw Newcastle’s lone striker, William Osula, isolated and even their normally imperious England left-back Lewis Hall given a thorough work out by Noni Madueke.

Much to Arteta’s chagrin, Lewis Miley, preferred to González in the midfield holding role, endeavoured to slow the tempo but the red tide could only be stemmed for so long.

According to recent reports, when Havertz dispossessed Hall after the latter miscontrolled a long ball, he cut inside and slid a highly intelligent, beautifully calibrated, pass across to the on-rushing Eberechi Eze. Without breaking stride, Eze exhibited perfect balance and unleashed a gorgeous first-time shot that arrowed, inexorably, past Hornicek.

• Arsenal ended a 21-game run of Premier League games without a draw (W18 D3) since a 2-2 draw with Wolves back in February.

• Since the start of last season, all five of Newcastle’s Premier League draws at St James’ Park have been a 2-2 scoreline.

In a recent development, • Eberechi Eze’s opener for Arsenal (pictured) was his first Premier League goal since April, which also put the Gunners 1-0 ahead against Newcastle. Opta.

As the home fans fell eerily silent, Arteta and his staff celebrated a goal sufficiently special to rebuke suggestions that his side are all about efficiency at the expense of artistry these days.

It has been revealed that with Declan Rice always available to reinforce his defence and smother any flickering home attack it proved a struggle to recall Newcastle making a meaningful attacking touch inside Arsenal’s box. Fans stationed near the home dugouts told Jaissle what they thought of it all.

It has been revealed that arsenal’s pressing was initially so good that Newcastle were left almost incapable of playing short passes and, instead found themselves reduced to aimless long balls. With Rice and Martin Ødegaard apparently operating on a different midfield planet an equaliser felt like a distant dream.

Yet that seemingly ambitious vision was something Harvey Barnes proved fully capable of buying into. When, early in the second half, Ødegaard made an uncharacteristic error, his heavy touch sliced the ball in Osula’s direction and the Dane played it into Barnes’s path.

All that remained was for the left winger to take a single, steadying, touch before an assured finish left the hitherto redundant David Raya picking his shot out of the net.

Jaissle’s second-half introduction of Tino Livramento, Jacob Ramsey and Anthony Elanga – all at Newcastle last season – at the expense of Dedic, Steur and Jacob Murphy was paying dividends. Suddenly, almost astonishingly, Arsenal were the team in danger of being pressed into submission.

The home side were closing their guests down far higher up the pitch and had morphed into an infinitely more menacing team. Soon, they were ahead when a Hall corner was headed down by Dan Burn, allowing Malick Thiaw to stab the ball beyond Raya.

Sources indicate that shortly afterwards Arsenal’s goalkeeper was helped off the pitch in evident pain after sustaining a nasty left shoulder injury during an ostensibly benign collision with Osula. On came Kepa Arrizabalaga in a triple substitution also featuring Guimarães’s exit.

Madueke though was still around and he reminded everyone of his presence by meeting the counterattacking Ødegaard’s fine pass, dummying two defenders and watching his slightly deflected shot evade Hornicek’s grasp.

In a recent development, no matter; Jaissle had done enough to win plenty of hearts and minds. Not least the chair, Yasir al-Rumayyan, over from Riyadh to watch his first match of the season and reportedly “take the club’s temperature”.

#70741. Don Bluth on the future of animation and AI: Thats definitely a road I dont want to travel on

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1741 w)

Don Bluth on the future of animation and AI: Thats definitely a road I dont want to travel on

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1741 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mashable

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For children of the '80s and '90s, Don Bluth was a major influence on how we saw the world.
  • Social media is evergreen with fans remembering the tender moments of Littlefoot and his tree star, or the terrifying ones, like Fievel or Mrs.
  • Sources indicate that in an interview with Mashable, Bluth said watching the finished doc "brought tears to [his] eyes," because it refreshed memories of his colleagues.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For children of the '80s and '90s, Don Bluth was a major influence on how we saw the world. With movies like The Secret of NIMH, An American Tail, The Land Before Time, All Dogs Go to Heaven, and Anastasia, this American animator offered us realms of adventure, with plucky heroes as well as villains so fantastically frightening that we carry the thrill of it all with us decades later.

Social media is evergreen with fans remembering the tender moments of Littlefoot and his tree star, or the terrifying ones, like Fievel or Mrs. Brisby being chased down by monstrous, roaring, ravenous cats. Now, for fans new and old, filmmakers Dave LaMattina and Chad N. Walker offer Don Bluth: Somewhere Out There, a documentary that explores the life and work of the innovative animator through his own words.

Sources indicate that in an interview with Mashable, Bluth said watching the finished doc "brought tears to [his] eyes," because it refreshed memories of his colleagues. Together, they pursued animation not for the money but for the art and a deep desire to create something meaningful for future generations. Yet, when asked about his legacy, Bluth is quick to look back on the path that led him to his work.

Recent findings suggest that he began by speaking of Winsor McCay, the father of American animation. In a wistful storyteller tone, Bluth recounted how a little boy witnessed the "magic" of the 1914 short film Gertie the Dinosaur, in which a pencil-sketched brontosaurus comes to life. This little boy was so inspired that he'd grow up to make his own animated short featuring a mouse named Mickey.

Recent findings suggest that that little boy, of course, was Walt Disney, who would go on to make 1937's Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs, the first animated feature film produced in the United States. That movie would go on to inspire a young Bluth, who'd direct his first animated feature in 1982 with The Secret of NIMH.

This path of inspiration to iconic art wasn't as direct a line as you might think.

Yes, Bluth scored a dream job, working at Disney Animation studio for 10 years on films like Sleeping Beauty, Robin Hood, and The Rescuers. But after Disney's death in 1966, Bluth and 17 other Disney animators feared the studio had lost their way, creatively.

He told Mashable he'd invite these artists to his home on weekends, where they'd draw together to develop innovative pitches for their corporate bosses. When they were shot down, Bluth — along with Gary Goldman and John Pomeroy — built their own firm, Don Bluth Productions, to "see if we could do better than they were doing." For this, Bluth remembered, "We were called traitors.".

In a recent development, that's not how Bluth saw his team. "[These] wonderful people had the courage to leave their jobs and security and go out there and try and do something great," he said, "not just to feed their egos, but something they felt helped them grow up. And they wanted to give back.".

It was not an easy journey, as Don Bluth: Somewhere Out There details, revealing the highs and lows of Bluth's most beloved and worst-reviewed productions, as well as the wildly popular video game Dragon's Lair. In our interview, he spoke repeatedly about how the doc filled him with gratitude as he looked back for the filmmakers' interviews.

To Mashable, he reflected, "What happened after so many movies, All Dogs Go to Heaven, American Tail, working with Steven Spielberg on both of those pictures, and George Lucas [on The Land Before Time], [it] became really, really obvious to us that we were doing the right thing [by] writing the right stories, and trying to make something that would move people's lives for the better — not just to pat our own backs and say, 'Look what we did.' [We were making] something that would help maybe children grow up and have some degree of morality about them. So then, that was our goal in everything.".

In Somewhere Out There, the rise of computer animation — which Bluth refers to as "3D animation" — came as a devastating blow to the animator, who'd spent his life developing the skills of hand-drawn 2D animation. To this day, Bluth still advocates for the artistry of hand-drawn animation.

"The way I look at this is animation in the 2D form is people, armed with a pencil in their hands, have to be able to draw," he explained, "and they also have to be able to act. And they have to have feelings about story.".

Recent findings suggest that to Bluth, CGI movies aren't animation. "3D animation is puppetry," he stated, adding, "[With 3D animation,] you drop your pencil. You put your hands on a keyboard, and you make a wireframe puppet act.".

Recent findings suggest that bluth shared several of his complaints about the look of 3D animation, saying, "To me, it looks very plastic... The colors are muted, and they're trying to put shading in there, trying to look more like a live-action picture." He asked, "Why are we trying to get to a place which looks more real?" adding, "That isn't the purpose at all of 2D [animation]. The purpose is to take you to a magical world. 2D is trying to make audiences come to our own world.".

It has been revealed that noting the animation industry changed forever with the massive success of 1995's Toy Story, Bluth mentioned, "Toy Story [movies] were quite fun to watch, but they didn't make me feel anything very deep. And animation is intended to do that, particularly with Walt Disney pictures. Snow White, Bambi, [and] Pinocchio — those pictures did something to change the way you thought and help you grow up in a way that was really good. And they did it in such a beautiful way.".

Recent findings suggest that it was when Disney Studios, post-Walt, moved away from these tenets that Bluth and his colleagues set out on their own. He said, "We left the Disney Studio because it was leaving out the morality statements and leaving out all the beautiful colors and everything.".

In terms of what recent animated films impressed Bluth, he said, "I liked Klaus a lot," commending Sergio Pablos' inventive Christmas tale, which employs hand-drawn animation with a unique visual style.

Bluth also enjoyed Pete Docter's 2009 Pixar hit Up. "That was totally in 3D," he noted, "but it had a great story. For my taste, it went on too long. You know, the story was really about this couple promising each other they would go back to some place in their life, and she died. So, the man, true to the promise, tries to fulfill that [by taking their house on the journey]. So, I love that.".

Recent findings suggest that overall though, Bluth lamented, "Animation has become an advertisement for sugar cereal and whatever. There are more advertisements on animation than there are actually animated characters. The animated characters are just simply little puppets that jump up and down and tell one-line jokes. So, that's not good. Now, the last laugh is about to hit us like a tsunami; that is AI.".

Recent findings suggest that through the stories of Russian Jewish immigrant Fievel Mousekewitz, the widowed mother of four Mrs. Brisby, the orphaned brontosaurus Littlefoot, and rogue mutt Charlie B. Barkin, Bluth was striving to create stories that would inspire children to be good and creative, as Disney's movies had done for him. He doesn't see a future where AI can provide such mindful, moral guidance.

Sources indicate that "It seems like AI is able to do wonderful, wonderful things," Bluth mused, "except AI is a machine, and it has no soul. It will borrow or steal, if you will, from everything that it knows, and give you what you ask for. But where's the creativity?".

In a recent development, "AI is a borrower," Bluth explained. "When you enter what you'd like to see, it searches all over and borrows it from other artists, puts it together. It indicates you on screen. Now, you can then make corrections. It can do all that, but it is still a machine. It doesn't ask you, 'Well, what is right and wrong? What is evil and good? What do you want me to say?' The machine can't do that.".

Recent findings suggest that he continued, "The only thing you can do is go back to human beings and say, 'Don't replace human beings with machines.' They're the ones who have a heart, who have a soul, and probably have a Creator. So, there's a bigger picture that's going on than just animation on a screen.".

"AI has no soul," Bluth concluded. "It hasn't a clue how to write anything. Everything that you're going to see on your screen has been stolen from other artists.".

In a recent development, he allowed that some AI might be "stunningly beautiful," but "you'll find that it doesn't affect your heart the way you feel… They're not artists that are doing the AI. Many of them don't understand the art of acting or anything. So, what everything looks like in AI animation that I've seen, it all looks like slow motion, and it looks unreal. So, that's definitely a road I don't want to travel on.".

"I read somewhere where someone mentioned something that stuck in my head," he mused, paraphrasing Oscar Wilde's The Portrait of Dorian Gray. "There are many people who know the price of everything but the value of nothing. And I certainly hope that's not where we're going.".

#70740. AI in classrooms: Fighting the great 'dumbing down'

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1387 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dw ↗ Open Full Page

AI in classrooms: Fighting the great 'dumbing down'

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1387 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that jakob is 15 years old and attends a secondary school for more academic students, known in Germany as a gymnasium.
  • "I had a French test today, and yesterday I had ChatGPT explain a lot of the topics to me again," the student told DW.
  • Math, German, English, chemistry and even physics: In one click, the solution or the path to a solution is available thanks to AI.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that jakob is 15 years old and attends a secondary school for more academic students, known in Germany as a gymnasium. He and his classmates have already been using artificial intelligence-enabled tools, or AI, for the last two and a half years.

"I had a French test today, and yesterday I had ChatGPT explain a lot of the topics to me again," the student told DW. Jakob isn't his real name, because he doesn't want to publicly admit he and many others of his age use AI to do their homework.

Math, German, English, chemistry and even physics: In one click, the solution or the path to a solution is available thanks to AI.

In science, this is called "cognitive outsourcing." Basically, the required thinking is shifted to another device, whether that's a calculator, notepad or a large language model (LLM) like ChatGPT.

There's a difference with AI, though. A notepad or calculator can take over a step or two but rarely the whole thought process. That's not the same for an LLM, which can handle the entire problem-solving process.

Jakob admitted he's also had an AI help him with his homework. "But only when I was really stuck," he insisted. And he's also aware that it can become a problem when AI does all your homework. "The students who get good grades tend not to do that," he explained.

Industry observers note that franziska Müller has been a German teacher for several decades and is currently teaching senior classes at a gymnasium. Her name has also been changed for privacy reasons.

"They can't even think for themselves anymore," she told DW, complaining about some of her classes.

Even in ordinary classes, some of the students type their questions into their tablets or phones, asking for AI assistance. And should they be called upon in class, she knows that they're reading out the answers that the AI has prepared for them and hoping nobody notices.

Müller believes students these days are less able to comprehend text. "Because they read less and let AI summarize almost everything for them," she remarked.

Several studies have reached very similar conclusions.

That includes the latest PISA (Program for International Student Assessment) study from September. PISA, which is run by the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development, regularly evaluates the abilities of 15-year-old students around the world.

Industry observers note that "Students who report using AI chatbots get lower scores in science, on average, than those who don't use AI," Andreas Schleicher, the OECD director for education and skills, wrote in his report in October. "This includes using AI to summarize texts they had to read, conduct preliminary research on a new topic, or draft texts for writing assignments.".

With participants from more than 90 countries, PISA is considered the largest international comparative study of 15-year-olds worldwide. This year, German 15-year-olds posted their lowest PISA scores in the 25-year history of the study.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

"The connections are complex and depend heavily on how generative AI is used, but the central insight is simple: Just as we don't get fit by watching sports but by doing sports ourselves, learning doesn't come from consuming content, but from the mind's productive cognitive engagement with newly introduced material," Schleicher explained.

Put simply, those who don't exercise their brains risk becoming less intelligent.

US think tank, the Brookings Institution, has already argued that the risks of using AI in education outweigh the benefits.

Its own research, which included young participants from around the world, speaks of students losing "fundamental cognitive and durable skills as they increasingly rely on AI to perform learning's intellectual work," as well as the decline of critical thinking, memory, perseverance and independent judgment.

But what can be done against the power of ChatGPT, Claude, Grok, Gemini and Meta AI?

Fresh York Mayor Zohran Mamdani has banned the use of AI in public schools up to the eighth grade for the 2026 and 2027 school years — so that's up to about the age of 14 or 15.

Not everyone agrees this is the right thing to do. Julian Hinn, who teaches German to students aged between 15 and 18 in Germany, said class members can still use AI apps on their mobile phones. "And anyone who thinks they won't use it at home is ignoring reality," Hinn told DW.

Germany's annual JIM study, which tracks teenagers' media use and device ownership, supports that view.

91% of young people surveyed in Germany, between the ages of 12 and 19, stated that they use at least one AI application. The study also reports that 74% use AI for homework and learning.

The last JIM study actually dates back to 2024 so those percentages might be even higher now. Data on AI use in Asia, Latin America and the US from the Brookings study show similarly high figures.

German politicians have recognized the problem. Although education in Germany is the responsibility of the individual federal states, the so-called Standing Conference of the Ministers of Education and Cultural Affairs, or KMK, has been issuing statements on the use of AI since 2024.

The KMK's statements have been rather vague though, saying only that students should be enabled to engage with AI in a critical, reflective and responsible manner.

Teachers and students alike are aware that AI can be a powerful support in the classroom.

"The AIs simply explain things much better than textbooks," said Jakob, adding that he'll often get an AI to explain basic concepts to him.

Sometimes teachers can't respond like an AI, Hinn conceded. "The AI ​​can respond much better to the language and needs of the students.".

That's why he thinks it's crucial to include AI in classes, starting from the 10th grade when students are around 15 or 16. Hinn doesn't think it should be introduced before that, when children's basic skills are still being developed.

In more senior classes, Hinn will encourage his students to question the AI critically. "We look at the quality of the solutions," he explained.

According to recent reports, german teacher Müller has also integrated some use of AI into her lessons for older students. But in some aspects of the class, she also bans it altogether so that her students can focus on thinking for themselves.

"I understand very well that it's tempting to use AI," she mentioned.

There are also other problems with AI in education. According to the Brookings study, students with basic skills can use AI to deepen their learning and progress faster.

But for children with gaps in their knowledge, they tend to adopt AI's errors, outsource their thinking and then fall even further behind. In this way, AI can exacerbate preexisting inequalities.

The PISA study notes that children from more affluent backgrounds often have a better start, and AI can widen that gap.

This is called the Matthew effect — the name comes from the biblical verse Matthew 25:29, "for unto everyone that hath shall be given." It basically means that early success in learning leads to better progress in the future, while early struggles equal a growing lag over time.

In the age of AI, teachers have become more motivated to challenge students to think independently and to consider their own personal autonomy.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Hinn, who also supervises the school newspaper, noted: "I always tell everyone, you can use AI but the feeling of having written an article with your own pen is spectacular.".

Both teachers also stress the idea of personal autonomy and responsibility. They believe this affects the students, especially because when they sit exams, they aren't allowed to use any aids or AI. And if they aren't able to solve their own problems, they will fail.

It's during exam time that the students really find out if they can solve those math, English or science problems by themselves.

Müller noted one of her students recently confessed they were upset after a poor exam result. "He felt he simply couldn't think for himself anymore because of AI," she said.

#70738. Breaking: A simple supplement could help your immune system fight cancer and viral infections

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1816 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: A simple supplement could help your immune system fight cancer and viral infections

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1816 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that A common amino acid found in everyday foods could play a surprisingly vital role in helping the immune system recognize cancer and fight viral infections.
  • Arginine is an amino acid that the body produces naturally and also obtains from protein-rich foods.
  • Now, fresh research suggests that restoring arginine levels could help the immune system respond more effectively to serious threats.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that A common amino acid found in everyday foods could play a surprisingly vital role in helping the immune system recognize cancer and fight viral infections. Scientists at Rockefeller University have discovered that when the body runs low on arginine, a key part of its immune defense system can stop working properly, potentially allowing dangerous cells and viruses to escape detection.

Arginine is an amino acid that the body produces naturally and also obtains from protein-rich foods. It is essential for making proteins that perform countless functions throughout the body. Researchers have long known that unusually low arginine levels are associated with several diseases, including colon cancer, but exactly how this shortage affects the body's defenses has remained unclear.

Now, fresh research suggests that restoring arginine levels could help the immune system respond more effectively to serious threats. In experiments involving mice, increasing dietary arginine reduced the formation of colon cancer tumors and lessened the severity of influenza and SARS-CoV-2 infections. Remarkably, providing arginine after mice had already contracted influenza also improved their outcomes.

According to recent reports, the findings, published in the journal Cell, raise the possibility that an inexpensive, readily available supplement could eventually become a useful addition to cancer treatments and strategies for combating viral infections. However, further research in humans is needed to determine whether the benefits observed in mice translate into effective treatments for people.

How a Missing Nutrient Could Help Cancer Escape the Immune System.

Recent findings suggest that the research was led by Sohail Tavazoie, who directs the Elizabeth and Vincent Meyer Laboratory of Systems Cancer Biology at Rockefeller University. His team has spent years investigating how arginine influences cancer development and progression.

In 2023, the researchers discovered that depriving colon cancer cells of arginine caused them to accumulate more genetic mutations. These changes can contribute to the unpredictable behavior of cancer cells, raising important questions about how arginine shortages might influence the disease.

The latest study reveals another potentially significant consequence. When arginine becomes scarce, cells struggle to produce enough of a crucial immune system protein known as MHC-1. This protein acts as a warning system, helping immune cells identify potential dangers such as cancerous changes or viral infections.

Without enough MHC-1, abnormal or infected cells may become harder for the immune system to recognize.

Encouragingly, the researchers also found that supplying a moderate amount of arginine, comparable to the quantity available in a couple of over-the-counter supplement tablets, could help restore production of this important protein.

Industry observers note that "Our work reveals how a lack of arginine interferes with the immune system, and suggests that upping arginine intake could prove beneficial," claims first author Qiushuang Wu, a postdoc in the lab. "Perhaps that means it could be used in combination with other therapies to treat both cancer and viral infections.".

Sources indicate that "Arginine supplementation could be readily tested in patients receiving immunotherapies or given to high-risk populations exposed to viral pathogens," Tavazoie suggests. "Considering that arginine is inexpensive and readily available, we hope that therapeutic and preventative studies could be undertaken soon.".

The Surprising Connection Between Arginine and Immune Defenses.

To understand why arginine has such an important effect, the researchers investigated how cells use amino acids to manufacture proteins.

According to recent reports, proteins are built from amino acids according to genetic instructions encoded in DNA. These instructions are copied into messenger RNA, which carries the information to the cellular machinery responsible for protein production.

Recent findings suggest that the instructions are read in groups of three genetic letters called codons. Each codon specifies an amino acid or provides another signal needed during protein production. Arginine is unusual in that six different codons can specify it, reflecting the multiple ways its incorporation into proteins can be encoded.

Scientists already knew that changes in amino acid availability could affect cellular metabolism and signaling, two processes that help regulate how cells obtain energy and respond to their surroundings. What remained less clear was whether shortages of particular amino acids could directly influence which proteins cells produce.

According to recent reports, to investigate, Wu examined the effects of arginine availability across several disease models, including colon cancer, influenza, and SARS-CoV-2. Each of these diseases has previously been associated with abnormal levels of various amino acids.

The research was supported in part by the Stavros Niarchos Foundation (SNF) Institute for Global Infectious Disease Research at The Rockefeller University and the Weill Cancer East Hub.

"One of the most dramatic patterns to emerge was that arginine was the most depleted amino acid in all of these diseases," she says.

Why Low Arginine Levels Can Disrupt the Immune System.

In laboratory experiments using cultured cells, Wu examined how arginine shortages affected protein production. She identified 414 proteins whose levels dropped abnormally when arginine was scarce.

Many of these proteins were associated with biological functions already known to depend on arginine. However, the researchers uncovered a more unexpected effect involving three genes from the HLA family.

These genes provide instructions for producing proteins associated with MHC-I (major histocompatibility complex class I), an essential component of the immune system's ability to recognize threats.

Sources indicate that MHC-I proteins are displayed on the surfaces of cells throughout the body. They act somewhat like identification displays, presenting small fragments of proteins from inside the cell to immune cells known as T cells.

When these displays reveal suspicious material, such as proteins produced by a virus or abnormal proteins associated with cancer, T cells can recognize the danger and help coordinate an immune response.

But the researchers found that arginine deficiency interfered with the production of these molecular warning signals.

The reason involved ribosomes, the tiny cellular machines that assemble proteins by following genetic instructions. Because the proteins involved in MHC-I production require arginine at numerous points, the researchers suspected that an insufficient supply could interfere with their assembly.

Industry observers note that further experiments confirmed that suspicion. When arginine was unavailable, ribosomes stalled while trying to manufacture MHC-I proteins. Without enough of the required amino acid, the cells could not efficiently complete the process.

According to recent reports, as a result, fewer MHC-I proteins reached the cell surface, reducing the signals that would normally alert T cells to cancer-associated or viral proteins. This created an opportunity for dangerous cells to avoid immune detection.

According to recent reports, "These findings are exciting because they reveal that consumption of a specific amino acid can directly regulate gene expression in an organism by increasing production of a protein enriched in that amino acid," Tavazoie says. "We believe that such selective translational tuning of gene expression through dietary manipulation likely extends to many other proteins and amino acids.".

More Arginine Meant Fewer Colon Cancer Tumors in Mice.

After identifying the molecular mechanism, Wu investigated whether changing the amount of arginine in an animal's diet could influence disease outcomes.

According to recent reports, mice receiving diets low in arginine developed more colon cancer tumors. In contrast, mice consuming higher amounts of the amino acid developed fewer tumors.

These findings provided evidence that arginine availability can influence cancer development through its effects on the immune system, rather than simply changing how individual cancer cells behave.

The results also raised a broader question: If arginine helps immune cells recognize cancer, could it provide similar benefits when the body encounters dangerous viruses?

Arginine Also Improved Outcomes From Influenza and COVID-19 Viruses.

To explore that possibility, Wu collaborated with Heinz-Heinrich Hoffman, a research assistant professor in Charles Rice's Laboratory of Virology and Infectious Disease.

Together, they examined the effects of dietary arginine in mouse models of influenza and SARS-CoV-2, the virus responsible for COVID-19.

The findings followed the same general pattern seen in the colon cancer experiments. Mice consuming more arginine experienced less severe symptoms from viral infections, suggesting that adequate levels of the amino acid helped support the body's immune defenses.

The researchers then made an even more surprising discovery.

Sources indicate that arginine did not appear to be beneficial only when consumed before an infection. Giving mice additional arginine after they had already been infected with influenza also improved their outcomes.

"Not only did mice with an arginine-rich diet have milder symptoms from viral infections, giving the mice arginine after influenza infection improved their outcomes too," Wu notes. "That was very surprising. From our genetic models, we knew manipulating arginine levels had a strong effect on gene expression, but we didn't expect the dietary manipulation to be equally impactful.".

The observation suggests that changing nutrient availability might influence how the immune system responds even after a viral infection has taken hold.

Could a Simple Supplement Improve Cancer and Virus Treatments?

The discovery has potentially important implications for understanding why some people become more vulnerable to cancer and severe viral infections.

Arginine levels naturally decline with age, and inadequate nutrition can further reduce the amount available to cells. The researchers suspect that these changes may contribute to the weakening of immune defenses seen in certain diseases and in older adults.

"Qiushuang's findings illuminate how poor diet and aging -- during which arginine levels naturally decline -- could create the perfect storm for the initiation of colon cancer. Similarly, age-related arginine loss could partially contribute to the greater mortality caused by respiratory viruses," Tavazoie says. "We're also investigating whether making dietary changes in other amino acids has beneficial effects in a variety of disease contexts. There are no doubt more discoveries to come.".

The possibility of using arginine alongside existing cancer immunotherapies is particularly intriguing. These treatments work by helping the immune system recognize and attack cancer cells. If low arginine levels interfere with the molecular signals required for that recognition, restoring the nutrient might help some treatments work more effectively.

The researchers also see potential for investigating arginine supplementation in people at elevated risk of respiratory viral infections.

Sources indicate that for now, these possibilities remain experimental. The findings do not establish that taking arginine supplements prevents or treats cancer, influenza, or COVID-19 in humans.

It has been revealed that nevertheless, the research reveals an important connection between nutrition and immunity. Rather than simply providing the raw materials needed to build proteins, specific amino acids may help determine how effectively the body's immune defenses identify and respond to dangerous threats.

And because arginine is inexpensive and widely available, the discovery could provide a practical starting point for future studies aimed at strengthening the immune system against cancer and infectious diseases.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to recent reports, net zero is no longer enough.
  • Scientists say that climate ‘overshoot’ — exceeding 1.5 °C of warming, a target set in 2015 in the landmark Paris Agreement — is now inevitable in the next few years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A display reminds those attending the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, of their goal: limiting global warming to 1.5 ºC.Credit: Metin Aktas/Anadolu/Getty.

According to recent reports, net zero is no longer enough. Among countries at the COP31 climate summit under way in Antalya, Turkey, there’s a growing recognition that meeting climate targets will require the world to go ‘net negative’, which means removal of more carbon dioxide from the air than is added.

Scientists say that climate ‘overshoot’ — exceeding 1.5 °C of warming, a target set in 2015 in the landmark Paris Agreement — is now inevitable in the next few years. Reaching net-zero status would halt the rise in temperatures. But only achieving net-negative status can bring temperatures back below the 1.5 °C threshold this century.

Recent findings suggest that can AI actually help the climate? Nations want to harness the technology to cut emissions.

Industry observers note that can AI actually help the climate? Nations want to harness the technology to cut emissions.

That reality has made net negative and the enormous amount of CO2 removal that would be needed to achieve it a prominent idea at the summit. A coalition of eight countries called the Group of Negative Emitters (GONE) has been working to convince other nations to adopt net-negative targets and get serious about CO2 removal. The group revealed that it will be co-chaired by Denmark and Ethiopia, which is hosting next year’s climate summit and could put net negative at the top of the agenda.

“We are in an era of overshoot, and we have to do a lot in terms of removing carbon dioxide,” Ethiopian ambassador Samuel Addis Alemayehu mentioned at a GONE event on 18 November, touting the nation’s progress on reforestation.

Recent findings suggest that some climate campaigners worry that CO2 removal technologies won’t work and that focusing on them could distract countries from cutting emissions. Despite those concerns, the latest draft of the main statement from COP31 recognizes that CO2 removal has a role in addressing the overshoot, and welcomes efforts to “urgently and rapidly” scale up development of removal methods.

According to a United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) report1 released ahead of the meeting, the world can expect about 1.8 °C of warming this century, even in the most optimistic emissions scenario.

Sources indicate that every fraction of a degree above 1.5 °C raises the risk of climate disasters such as wildfires and powerful hurricanes. “COP31 will be judged a failure if we don’t address the overshoot,” said Ilana Seid, Palau’s ambassador to the UN and chair of the Association of Small Island States, at a press briefing held during the summit.

In a recent development, many countries at the meeting have discussed slashing emissions to limit the size and duration of the coming overshoot. Turkey has pushed to implement a target of 35% of global energy demand being met with electricity by 2035, a proposal that has gained support from more than 75 countries at the conference and is also included in the draft statement.

Sources indicate that but the UNEP report estimates that to recover from overshoot, at least 330 billion tonnes of CO2 would have to be pulled out of the atmosphere this century after the world reaches net zero. Removing that much CO2 would require a vast expansion of existing efforts. Today, about two billion tonnes of CO2 per year are removed by nature-based projects such as reforestation, which takes advantage of the carbon absorbed by growing trees. Scaling up carbon removal quickly enough to achieve net negative and storing carbon in a more durable form will require technological CO2 removal solutions as well.

Muse Is Unleashing a World of Pettiness on Instagram

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (773 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Khalil Roberts had heard horror stories of people getting kicked off Instagram for using third-party apps to purge follower counts, so when he came across an X post claiming that Muse—Meta’s AI assistant—could mass-unfollow people who didn’t follow him back, he didn’t believe it.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Khalil Roberts had heard horror stories of people getting kicked off Instagram for using third-party apps to purge follower counts, so when he came across an X post claiming that Muse—Meta’s AI assistant—could mass-unfollow people who didn’t follow him back, he didn’t believe it.

“I’ve never gone through my exact list to vet those people out, but I’ve always been curious,” the 31-year-old New Yorker tells WIRED. But after realizing that by using Muse, his account wouldn’t get flagged as spam, his mind was made up. “I was like, I actually will be a little petty.”.

After downloading Muse, Roberts, who had over 7,600 followers, entered the prompt: “Can you show me a list of people (non celebrity) that [don’t] follow me back on instagram and can you unfollow them for me. ”.

Within minutes, Muse identified 151 accounts. It attached an Excel sheet with a breakdown of everyone cataloged—separated by categories identifying their username, real name, classification, and profile link—and asked if Roberts wanted to proceed with his request. Shockingly, some of the names were people he thought of as friends. “It was a little surprising, but also a reminder that we don’t have a relationship anymore.”.

Recent findings suggest that following the success of his November 7 cleanse, Roberts posted about it on X, offering instructions to his followers. Over the past several weeks, parallel scenarios have played out across X, Instagram, and Facebook, with customers sharing tips on how to automate their unfollows with the help of Muse.

Recent findings suggest that X user @justdrmj posted about the trend the same week as Roberts, and nearly every reply shared a taste for trivial grudge-holding. For him it came down to one simple rule: “Why be a fan?” “i agree. reciprocity is key,” one person said in response. “The way I just cleaned house,” added another. In a seeming outburst of celebration, one X user posted: “Just unfollowed 1000+ people on IG.”.

Even tech worker Kimberly Munoz, who has 33,200 Instagram followers, stated she wasn’t about to be “anybody’s fan,” noting in an Instagram video that she used the feature to suss out “people that I know in real life that have unfollowed me.” “I downloaded Muse just to do this only,” one person responded.

In a recent development, with social media rapidly evolving, there is no longer a unified consensus around etiquette. For some people, following others is an indication of friendship or simply a way to keep tabs on your latest crush. Others view it as more of a social obligation—you follow someone if they follow you, but the opposite is true as well.

Natalie Pennington, an associate professor who researches social connection at Colorado State University, wonders about the consequences of people gradually outsourcing small social decisions to technology.

“It is probably at least partially a question of not wanting to deal with emotionally uncomfortable things,” Pennington indicates. “This also strikes me as another example of information we don’t really need that social media can give us. There’s this data that exists at the platform level or would take a lot of effort to find out on your own, but now you can learn with the click of the button. But it doesn’t mean it is something you need to know.”.

In October, despite the seeming popularity of the feature, Meta removed an advertising campaign that promoted Muse with the promise that customers could “see who unfollowed you each week,” Business Insider reported.

When WIRED asked about the reasoning behind Meta’s decision to remove the ad, the company did not respond to a request for comment.

But Muse’s capabilities aren’t just being employed to even scores. Some people are using the assistant to streamline feeds that have become extremely cluttered over the years.

Elizabeth Brooks is a self-proclaimed “sweeper”—the term for a hobbyist who routinely enters sweepstakes and promotional contests—who, over the course of 10 years, had followed various accounts offering giveaways. Recently, she started prompting the assistant to bring her five profile links every few hours, no more than six times a day, for her to manually unfollow one by one. “Your following list can finally work for you instead of the other way around,” she wrote on Facebook.

Industry observers note that roberts, who joined Instagram in high school 15 years ago and calls the platform “my app of choice,” says people are becoming more intentional about their digital relationships and who they let into their online lives. But he doesn’t initiative on letting Muse make any more decisions about his social life, he says.

“Unfollowing is where I draw the line.”.
